opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #1177: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős, Galvin and Hajnal posed three statements about the families of 3-uniform hypergraphs of a given uncountable chromatic number that avoid a fixed finite one. In June 2026 Eric Li's paper on problem 593 claimed, as a consequence, that the three statements have the answers yes, no and yes. The paper and Lean development are the same as for problem 593, so a rerun there is a rerun here. Nobody independent has reported either. Everything here is open.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record: the problem page, the proof-claims thread, and every artifact the claimants made public, by commit or hash. Nothing has been run. On 2026-11-17 Nervous Machine wrote a reading guide that lays the third-party formal statements and the claimant's own beside the problem page, definition by definition, and records one question about which wording of the second assertion is the problem. The gaps that follow are the checks still owed.

cycles.spoken: Eric Li posted a paper on arXiv claiming to resolve problems 593 and 1177; the Erdős-problems AI wiki listed it as a candidate full solution, marked unverified. The proof claim was listed on the problem page with links to the paper and the formalisation. The Lean repository reached its current commit. The problem page lists one proof claim, not marked accepted by the site. A third-party formalisation of the problem statement exists.

preregistered.question: Can the open semantic gap (EG2) be made cheaper for a human reviewer: the three assertions as posed, the third-party and the claimant's formal statements, every definition behind them, a plain rendering, and the points to confirm; in particular, is each answer attached to the right statement and is the 'no' the true negation?
preregistered.rule: Statements quoted verbatim from files fetched read-only at pinned commits, with file and line; renderings marked as the agent's; every discrepancy recorded whether harmless or not, and an anomaly opened if it could change the meaning; worked examples written but not run, and no output claimed; standing unchanged by construction.
predictions: P1: the three formal-conjectures statements render to the page's three assertions with no quantifier mismatch; part ii is the true negation of assertion 2 with both hypotheses kept
P2: the claimant's statements render to the same assertions, part 2 the classical equivalent of the negation, but their agreement with formal-conjectures rests on definitions no machine has linked
P3: both use weak colouring, non-induced injective containment and vertex count; at least two conventions need a sentence; none changes the meaning

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine wrote the reading guide for the question on this record that a machine cannot settle: whether the formal statements of problem 1177 say what Erdős, Galvin and Hajnal asked, and whether the answers yes, no and yes are attached to the right ones. The guide quotes the problem page, the third-party formal statements and the claimant's own, which are two separate formalisations that no machine links, and traces every symbol to its definition with file and line. In the agent's reading both say what the page says, and the no is the true negation of the second assertion. One thing was not predicted: the claimant's paper says the 1999 source asked the first two assertions for uncountably chromatic systems, not for chromatic number exactly aleph one. For the no, the exact version is the weaker refutation, so if the older wording is the problem, the formal no does not settle it on its own; the paper's argument appears to give the stronger no, but no Lean statement says so. That is opened as anomaly A1. Seven small Lean checks are written but have not been run. The readings are the system's, not a mathematician's, so nothing changed standing. A set theorist can now sign or refuse five lines.

anomalies.node: EG2: formal statement of the second assertion
anomalies.spoken: The problem page and both formal statements read the second assertion for systems of chromatic number exactly aleph one. The claimant's paper says the 1999 source put it for uncountably chromatic systems. For the no answer the exact version is the weaker refutation: it does not by itself rule out a system of larger uncountable chromatic number avoiding both forbidden systems. The paper's argument appears to give the stronger no, through a result the development also formalises, but no Lean statement says so and nobody has checked it. If the older wording is the problem, the formal no does not settle the second assertion on its own.

evidence.source_wording: paper.tex l.268-271 (the claimant's account; the 1999 booklet was not consulted)

background.spoken: For a finite 3-uniform hypergraph G and a cardinal kappa, let F(G, kappa) be the 3-uniform hypergraphs of chromatic number kappa that do not contain G. Three statements: if F(G, aleph-one) is non-empty it contains one of size at most two to the power two to the power aleph-null; if F(G, aleph-one) and F(H, aleph-one) are both non-empty so is their intersection; and if kappa and lambda are uncountable and F(G, kappa) is non-empty then so is F(G, lambda).
